name: rgxg
desc: C library and command-line tool to generate (extended) regular expressions
why: Generates regular expressions from examples, a neat inversion of the usual regex workflow worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: rgxg (ReGular eXpression Generator) is a C library and a command-line tool that generate (extended) regular expressions. You give it a specification, such as a numeric range like 0 to 31 or 00 to FF, or a CIDR block like 192.168.0.0/24 or 2001:db8:aaaa::/64, and it outputs a regular expression that matches exactly that set. The homepage and README do not show the exact input syntax or sample output. The scout note says it generates regexes from examples, but the homepage describes range and CIDR inputs, not example strings, so the entry should not describe it as example-driven.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says rgxg can be useful for generating expressions that match a specific number range or all addresses in a CIDR block, which are awkward to write by hand. The README gives no further motivation.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the generation algorithm. It says rgxg is a C library with a command-line front end and produces (extended) regular expressions. Build and install steps are described, but not the internals.

brief.install_notes: Outside brew install, the README describes a build from source: a C compiler such as gcc, make, and for git checkouts autoconf, automake and libtool. Optional libcheck is needed only for 'make check' (LGPL-2.1). Run ./autogen.sh (git only), then ./configure, make, make install. The homepage also lists packages for apt, apk, AUR (yay -S rgxg), nix-env, and FreeBSD pkg. The homepage recommends verifying the PGP signature of a release or tag before use, and the README gives the maintainer's key fingerprint for comparison. The two pages list different key details: the homepage shows a 4096R key expiring 2021-06-27, the README an rsa4096 key expiring 2023-06-27.
brief.standout: Most regex tools go from pattern to matches. rgxg runs the other way: it writes a pattern from a numeric range or network block, which makes it handy for validating things like port ranges or CIDR membership. It is also a C library, so other programs can call it, not just a shell tool.
brief.status: quiet: the stable release 0.1.2 is dated 12 Apr 2020, the homepage was last updated 19 May 2024, and the README does not show a last commit date. The maintainer's key expiry dates on the two pages also disagree, which suggests the docs are not updated together.
brief.caveats: No release in several years, so you may be on an old version. The README does not document the input syntax, the output format, or the library API. The README only describes build steps and does not mention Windows. Build from source needs autotools if you use a git checkout. The signing key appears to have expired, so verify the fingerprint against another source before relying on signature checks. The scout note's claim about generating from examples is not supported by the homepage. The library version is fixed until a stable release.

entry.title: rgxg
entry.tldr: Writes the regular expression for you: give it a numeric range or a CIDR block and it prints a pattern matching exactly that set.
entry.deeper_look:
rgxg (ReGular eXpression Generator) is a C library with a small command-line front end. Instead of matching text against a pattern, it goes the other way. You describe a set, such as a number range like 0 to 31 or 00 to FF, or a network block like 192.168.0.0/24 or 2001:db8:aaaa::/64, and it produces an (extended) regular expression that matches exactly that set.

The reason is plain: these patterns are tedious and error-prone to write by hand. A regex for "0 to 31" or "any address in this /24" has to spell out digit-by-digit alternatives, and one slip lets bad input through. Generating the pattern from the specification turns a fiddly puzzle into a lookup.

The idea underneath is that a regular expression is just a compact description of a finite set, and for sets with structure, such as ranges and prefixes, a program can derive that description mechanically. It is a small door into how regexes encode numbers and addresses. Because it is also a library, other C programs can call it directly rather than shelling out.

The README does not document the input syntax or show sample output, so expect to learn it from the tool's own help.

entry.whats_unique: Most regex tools go from pattern to matches. rgxg runs the other way, writing a pattern from a numeric range or network block, and it ships as a C library as well as a shell tool.
entry.caveats: The last stable release, 0.1.2, is from April 2020, and the README does not document input syntax, output format, or the library API.
